Stage 3 · Grammar

If this really happens, then what?

A real possibility on one side, and what follows from it on the other.

Read these three sentences.
  • If a country has high taxes, it can provide free healthcare.
  • If you cycle for thirty minutes a day, it may add years to your life.
  • Unless you have close friendships, you will find it hard to be happy.
All three are about the future. So why is there no will after if or unless?
A conditional sentence has two halves, and the tenses show how likely the speaker thinks it is.

Every conditional sentence contains a condition (the if clause) and a result. What differs between the conditional types is not the logic but the tense pattern, and that pattern is how the speaker signals their judgement about how real the situation is.

The first or real conditional uses a present form in the condition and will in the result: If you eat a balanced diet, you’ll feel healthier. This combination says the speaker considers the condition a genuine possibility in the present or the future. It is the conditional of predictions, warnings, promises, offers and advice — anything you actually expect might happen.

Alongside it sits a closely related pattern with the present in both halves, sometimes called the zero conditional: If people enjoy their job, they are happier in general. This is not about one occasion at all; it states what is generally or scientifically true. The difference matters: If you heat water, it boils is a fact about water, while If you heat the soup, it’ll be ready in five minutes is a prediction about tonight.

One rule governs the whole family and is worth learning before anything else: no will in the if clause. The future is carried by the result clause alone. This is the same restriction that applies after when, as soon as, until, before and after, which you met in Lesson 5, and roughly nine out of ten first-conditional errors are exactly this.

Before you look at the table: the table below shows the two halves of the sentence in separate columns, so you can see which tense belongs on which side. Check the comma rule at the bottom too.
The two halves
 The conditionThe result
Formif + present simplewill / won’t + verb
Other results—may, might, can, could, should, tend to, an imperative
ExampleIf people work a 37-hour week,they will have a lot of leisure time.

CommaOnly when the if half comes first.—
Four words for the condition
WordMeansExample
ifon this conditionIf you exercise outdoors, you’ll work better.
unlessif… not — already negativeUnless you have close friends, you won’t be happy.
as long asonly on this conditionMoney helps as long as everyone has enough.
provided thatonly on this condition — more formalProvided that the society is balanced, people are content.

One rule covers most of it. No will after if. The present simple in the condition half already means the future: If it rains tomorrow…, never If it will rain tomorrow.

Unless is already negative. It means if…not. So do not make it negative twice: not Unless you don’t have friends but Unless you have friends.

The result half can be softer than will. may, might and could all fit: If you cycle every day, it may add years to your life. Use them when the result is likely rather than certain.

Do not confuse the comma rule with the meaning. If people work fewer hours, they have more time and People have more time if they work fewer hours mean exactly the same. Only the comma changes.

Full grammar reference — the real (first) conditional

What it is

A conditional sentence has two parts: an if clause naming a condition, and a result clause naming what follows from it. The real or first conditional is used when the condition is a genuine possibility in the present or future. Its standard shape is if + present simple, then will + base verb.

What it means, and what it does

The tense pattern is what marks the speaker’s attitude. By putting the condition in a present form and the result in will, you signal that you think this could really happen. Compare If people spend more than an hour travelling to work, they are less happy — a general truth — with If you take that job, you’ll spend two hours commuting, a real prediction about one person’s future.

When and why we use it

Every conditional sentence contains a condition (the if clause) and a result. What differs between the conditional types is not the logic but the tense pattern, and that pattern is how the speaker signals their judgement about how real the situation is.

The first or real conditional uses a present form in the condition and will in the result: If you eat a balanced diet, you’ll feel healthier. This combination says the speaker considers the condition a genuine possibility in the present or the future. It is the conditional of predictions, warnings, promises, offers and advice — anything you actually expect might happen.

Alongside it sits a closely related pattern with the present in both halves, sometimes called the zero conditional: If people enjoy their job, they are happier in general. This is not about one occasion at all; it states what is generally or scientifically true. The difference matters: If you heat water, it boils is a fact about water, while If you heat the soup, it’ll be ready in five minutes is a prediction about tonight.

One rule governs the whole family and is worth learning before anything else: no will in the if clause. The future is carried by the result clause alone. This is the same restriction that applies after when, as soon as, until, before and after, which you met in Lesson 5, and roughly nine out of ten first-conditional errors are exactly this.

Typical situations

You need the real conditional for giving advice and warnings, making offers and promises, negotiating (as long as you…), stating rules, and discussing what will happen if a plan goes ahead.

  • A likely future result — the core use: this may well happen.If you eat a balanced diet, you’ll feel healthier.
  • A general truth or a scientific fact — present in both clauses; sometimes called the zero conditional.If people enjoy their job, they are happier in general.
  • A warning — the result clause carries the consequence.If you spend more than you earn, you’ll end up in debt.
  • A promise or an offer — first person, future result.If you help me with this, I’ll buy you lunch.
  • Advice and instructions — imperative or a modal in the result clause.If you feel stressed, go outside for ten minutes.
  • A condition with a limit — as long as, provided that, on condition that stress the requirement.You can leave early as long as you finish the report.
  • A negative condition — unless = if not.Unless the government invests, nothing will change.

How it differs from similar structures

First conditional = a real possibility, present + will. Second conditional = imagined or unlikely, past + would. If I get the job, I’ll move (I might) vs If I got the job, I’d move (I doubt it). Lesson 23 develops this.
if = names a possibility · unless = names the exception · as long as = names a requirement. I’ll come if I can / unless I’m working / as long as you tell me the time.

How to build it

Standard: If + subject + present simple, + subject + will + base verb
Reversed: subject + will + base verb + if + subject + present simple  (no comma)
Zero conditional: If + present simple, + present simple
Other results: may / might / can / should + base verb, or an imperative
AffirmativeIf it rains, we’ll stay in.
Negative conditionIf he doesn’t come, we’ll start without him.
Negative resultIf you work reasonable hours, you won’t burn out.
QuestionWhat will you do if they offer you the job?
With a modal resultIf you save now, you might be able to buy a flat.
With an imperativeIf you feel ill, call the doctor.
Comma ruleComma only when the if clause comes first.
UnlessUnless already means if not: Unless you hurry, you’ll miss it.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • ’ll is almost inaudible in fast speech, so the result clause often sounds like a plain present. Listen for the vowel change: we stay /wiː steɪ/ vs we’ll stay /wil steɪ/.
  • If is unstressed; the stress falls on the condition itself: if you SPEND more than an hour…
  • In writing, the comma corresponds to a real pause after a fronted if clause.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • No will in the if clause. If it will rain is wrong. This is the same rule that governs when, as soon as, until, before, after (Lesson 5), and it is the single most frequent conditional error.
  • The result clause is not restricted to will. Any modal fits, and so does an imperative: If you see him, tell him to call me.
  • Unless cannot be used with a negative verb: Unless you don’t hurry means the opposite of what the speaker intends. Use unless + positive verb.
  • As long as, provided that and on condition that are stronger than if — they set a requirement rather than name a possibility.
  • In case is not a conditional: Take an umbrella in case it rains means ‘because it might rain’, not ‘if it rains’.
  • The zero conditional describes what is always true; the first conditional describes one specific future occasion. If you heat water, it boils vs If you heat the soup, it’ll be ready in five minutes.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • If it will rain, we’ll stay in. → If it rains, we’ll stay in.No will in the if clause.
  • Unless you don’t hurry, you’ll be late. → Unless you hurry, you’ll be late.Unless already contains the negative.
  • If you will be tired, go to bed. → If you’re tired, go to bed.The condition takes a present form.
  • If people spend more than an hour travelling, they will be less happier. → If people spend more than an hour travelling, they will be less happy.Less and -er cannot combine.
  • I’ll help you, if you need it. → I’ll help you if you need it.No comma when the if clause comes second.
  • If you would eat better, you’d feel healthier — and you can, easily. → If you eat better, you’ll feel healthier.A realistic condition takes the first conditional, not would.

More examples in context

  • predictionIf the cost of living keeps rising, fewer people will move to the capital.
  • general truthIf people have free childcare, more of them go back to work.
  • warningIf you spend more than an hour commuting each way, you’ll notice the difference.
  • promiseIf you cover Friday for me, I’ll take your Monday shift.
  • adviceIf you want to feel healthier, get outside every day.
  • modal resultIf the economy stays strong, wages may rise next year.
  • requirementYou can work from home as long as you attend the Monday meeting.
  • condition with providedThe company pays for training provided that you stay two years.
  • negative conditionUnless the country invests in healthcare, the figures won’t improve.
  • questionWhat will you do if they don’t offer you the salary you asked for?

A tip for remembering it

Say the pattern out loud until it is automatic: ‘if + present, will + verb’. Then check one thing only — is there a will on the wrong side of the comma? Nine out of ten first-conditional errors are exactly that. If you want to use unless, translate it first: unless = if … not, so the verb after it stays positive.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. The first conditional describes a real possibility: if + present simple, + will + base verb.
  2. Never put will in the if clause.
  3. The result clause can also take may, might, can, should or an imperative.
  4. Comma only when the if clause comes first.
  5. Unless = if not, so the verb after it is positive.
  6. As long as / provided that set a requirement; in case is not a conditional at all.

Stage 5 · Main input

The happiest country in the world

Denmark keeps winning. The reasons are not the ones people expect.

Before you read: a yearly report ranks countries by how satisfied their people say they are.

What do you think matters most?

Decide first. The last paragraph gives the researchers’ answer.

The happiest country in the world

Every year a report ranks the world by happiness, and every year the same small northern countries come out on top. The interesting part is not who wins. It is why.

ASince 2012, researchers have asked people in more than 150 countries a deceptively simple question. Imagine a ladder with ten steps. The top step is the best possible life for you; the bottom is the worst. Which step are you standing on today? The answers are averaged, and the result is published as the World Happiness Report. The Nordic countries have finished at or near the top almost every year since it began.

BThe obvious explanation is money, and it is partly right. If a country is very poor, its people report low satisfaction, and that changes quickly when incomes rise. But the relationship breaks down higher up the scale. Above a certain point, extra income makes surprisingly little difference. If a society is already comfortable, what raises satisfaction is not a bigger economy but a fairer one — and a lower gap between the richest and the poorest predicts happiness better than the national income does.

CSo the researchers look at six factors: income, healthy life expectancy, social support, freedom to make your own choices, generosity, and trust. That last one does most of the work. If you believe a lost wallet in your city would be returned to you, you will report a higher life satisfaction — and in the Nordic countries, unusually, most people do believe it. Denmark has repeatedly come near the top of that particular measure.

DWhat does this look like day to day? Free or very cheap childcare, so that having a child does not end a career. Healthcare that does not depend on your employer. Reasonable working hours: people tend to have more job satisfaction if they finish at a sensible time, and Danes spend a good deal of their leisure time socializing rather than working. Then there is hygge, a word with no exact English translation, which describes a particular cosy, unhurried kind of evening with friends and family.

ENone of this makes the model easy to copy, and it is not free. Taxes are high, and the whole arrangement depends on a level of trust in public institutions that takes generations to build and can be lost quickly. Critics also point out that the survey measures how content people say they are, not how content they are. If a culture is uncomfortable with complaining, its scores will look good whatever is really happening.

FPerhaps the most useful finding is the least glamorous. Across every country studied, the strongest single predictor of satisfaction is not wealth, weather or health, but whether people feel they have somebody to rely on in a crisis. Unless you have that, very little else compensates — and provided you do, a great deal can be survived. It is not a policy that any government can simply announce, which may be exactly why it is so often ignored.

Written for this course. Rankings and factors are drawn from the World Happiness Report, published annually by the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network.
